Nonmetric asymmetric MDS by the ellipse-distance (Model II) and radius-distance (Model III) models

Source: R/ellipse_mds.R
ellipse_mds.Rd

Okada and Imaizumi (1984; see Chino & Okada, 1996, Section 3.5) wrote the asymmetric proximity from object j to object k as m_jk = d_jk + alpha * c(j, k) + beta * c(k, j), where d_jk is the Euclidean distance between the points x_j and x_k, and named three families by how the asymmetric term c is restricted:

Usage

ellipse_mds(
  x,
  ndim = 2,
  model = c("II", "III", "I"),
  alpha = -1,
  beta = 1,
  type = c("similarity", "dissimilarity"),
  ndim_max = ndim,
  nrandom = 10,
  maxit = 2000,
  reltol = 1e-10,
  seed = 1,
  kappa = Inf,
  axis_max = Inf,
  check_orientation = TRUE,
  angles = c(10, 15, 20)
)

Arguments

x

A square matrix of asymmetric proximities. The diagonal is ignored; other missing cells are left out of the fit.

ndim

Number of dimensions.

model

"II" (ellipse-distance model, default) or "III" (radius-distance model). "I" is reserved and gives an error.

alpha, beta

Signs of the asymmetric terms of the object itself and of the other object, each -1, 0 or 1 (not both 0).

type

"similarity" (default) or "dissimilarity". If x has a type attribute set by as_proximity(), that is used.

ndim_max

Dimensionality at which the rational initial configuration is built; the solutions are reduced from there down to ndim.

nrandom

Number of random starts tried in addition to the rational start (0 uses the rational start only).

maxit, reltol

Passed to stats::optim().

seed

Random seed for the random starts. The state of the random number generator is restored afterwards. NULL uses (and advances) the current state of the generator.

kappa, axis_max

Model II only: optional upper bounds of the aspect ratio (max_t r_jt / min_t r_jt) and of the size (geometric mean of the semiaxes, in units of the root mean square distance of the points from the centroid) of each ellipse. The default Inf leaves them unbounded as in the original method. S hardly determines the shape of the ellipses: without bounds some ellipses can become very long and thin or very large while S decreases only slightly, and with bounds the solution usually sits on the bound. A warning is given when an unbounded solution has an aspect ratio above 10 or a size above 3, and when a bound is reached.

check_orientation

Logical; for Model II with ndim >= 2, compute S after rotating the semiaxis configuration (see Details).

angles

Rotation angles in degrees for check_orientation.

Value

An object of class c("mdspace_ellipse", "mdspace") with conf (n x ndim), semiaxis (n x ndim; Model II) or radius (Model III), stress (S), niter, mjk and disparity (n x n matrices, NA on the diagonal and missing cells), path (S at each dimensionality from ndim_max to ndim for the rational start), starts (S of each start, the rational one first), best_start, converged, model, alpha, beta, kappa, axis_max, at_bound (whether some ellipse reached kappa or axis_max), and orientation (a data frame with the dimensions, angle, and S after counterclockwise and clockwise rotation; NULL when not computed).

Details

  • Model II (ellipse-distance model; Okada, 1990): each object j has an ellipse (ellipsoid, hyperellipsoid) centered at x_j with semiaxes r_j1, ..., r_jp along the dimensions, and c(j, k) is the radius of the ellipse of j in the direction of k, rho_jk = d_jk v_jk with v_jk = 1 / sqrt(sum_t ((x_jt - x_kt) / r_jt)^2) (Okada & Imaizumi, 2024, Equations 3.10 to 3.13). When all semiaxes of j are equal to r_j, rho_jk = r_j and Model II reduces to Model III.

  • Model III (radius-distance model; Okada & Imaizumi, 1987): c(j, k) = r_j, the radius of a circle (sphere, hypersphere) centered at x_j.

  • Model I: the most general model, in which c depends on the pair of objects and the dimension. It is not implemented yet, because how it is restricted to be estimable is given only in Okada and Imaizumi (1984).

The signs alpha and beta give the submodels. The defaults alpha = -1, beta = 1 are the models used by Okada and Imaizumi (1987, 2024; Model IIIB): m_jk is the distance from the near edge of the ellipse (circle) of j to the far edge of that of k, and it is assumed to be monotonically decreasing in similarities (increasing in dissimilarities). With alpha = beta the model is symmetric (Saito's cluster model for Model III).

The fit is S = sqrt(sum((m_jk - mhat_jk)^2) / sum((m_jk - mbar)^2)) with disparities mhat_jk from monotone regression (primary approach to ties), as in circle_mds(). S is minimized over the coordinates and the semiaxes (radii) by stats::optim() (BFGS) with the analytic gradient, with the semiaxes parameterized by their logarithms so that they stay positive.

Initial values (Okada & Imaizumi, 2024, Section 5.4). The rational start is the Torgerson configuration of the symmetrized dissimilarities (with the additive constant) in ndim_max dimensions and the radii from the skew-symmetric part, which serve as initial semiaxes for all dimensions (a small constant is added so that no semiaxis is zero). The solution is reduced one dimension at a time down to ndim: for Model II by dropping the dimension with the smallest sum_j x_jt^2 + sum_j r_jt^2 (Equation 5.23), because the orientation of the dimensions is determined by the model; for Model III by projecting on the principal axes. nrandom random starts are also tried in ndim dimensions, because the models have local minima; a typical one for Model II puts most points near the origin with almost concentric ellipses (Section 5.3).

Normalization. The configuration is centered with the sum of squared coordinates equal to n, and the semiaxes (radii) are rescaled with it. For Model III the smallest radius is set to 0 (the radii are determined only up to an additive constant); the semiaxes of Model II have no such indeterminacy and are not shifted. The dimensions of Model II are not rotated, because rotating them changes S; they are ordered by decreasing variance of the coordinates. Model III is rotated to principal axes.

Orientation of dimensions (Model II). If the semiaxes of two dimensions are nearly equal for all objects (the points of the semiaxis configuration lie near the diagonal), the ellipses are nearly circles and the orientation of the two dimensions is not determined. As in Okada and Imaizumi (2024, Sections 3.1.2 and 4.1.2), for each pair of dimensions the semiaxis configuration is rotated by angles degrees counterclockwise and clockwise, the coordinates are refitted with the rotated semiaxes fixed (starting from the solution), and the resulting S is reported. If it is clearly larger than the S of the solution, the orientation is uniquely determined up to permutations and reflections of the dimensions.

References

Okada, A. (1990). A generalization of asymmetric multidimensional scaling. In M. Schader & W. Gaul (Eds.), Knowledge, data and computer-assisted decisions (pp. 127-138). Springer.

Okada, A., & Imaizumi, T. (1987). Nonmetric multidimensional scaling of asymmetric proximities. Behaviormetrika, 14(21), 81-96.

Okada, A., & Imaizumi, T. (2024). Applied multidimensional scaling of asymmetric relationships. Springer.

千野直仁・岡太彬訓 (1996). 非対称多次元尺度構成法とその周辺. 行動計量学, 23(2), 130-152.

See also

circle_mds() for Model IIIB with the two-mode three-way extension.

Examples

x <- matrix(c(NA, 5, 2, 1, 3,
              3, NA, 4, 2, 2,
              1, 2, NA, 6, 3,
              2, 1, 4, NA, 5,
              4, 2, 2, 3, NA), 5, byrow = TRUE)
fit <- ellipse_mds(x, ndim = 2, nrandom = 2)
fit
#> mdspace: ellipse

#>   1-2    15           0.0781    0.0553
